subject: Mathematics
source: National Curriculum / EYFS Early Learning Goals (Number; Numerical Patterns); Drive KS3 material not applicable at this age

lessons.title: Counting objects to 5
objectives: Count up to 5 objects, touching each one once
Say the number names 1 to 5 in order

keywords.def: say the number names in order, one for each thing
a word or symbol that tells us how many

starter: Say Bismillah together, then wiggle your fingers: how many fingers on one hand?
Clap three times. Can you clap three times again?
Sing or say the numbers 1 to 5 with your fingers.

teach.heading: Let's count dates
bullets: Here are 3 dates on a plate.
Touch each date as we count.
teach.note: Show 3 real or pictured dates. Model pointing to each object once. Ask: what is the last number we said? Emphasise the last number tells us how many.

teach.heading: One touch for one thing
bullets: Move each thing as you count it.
Do not count the same thing twice.
teach.note: Deliberately count one object twice and ask children to spot the mistake. Common misconception: counting the same object twice or saying numbers faster than touching.

teach.heading: Count to 5
teach.note: Use screen sharing with moving counters. Invite individual children to unmute and count while you move the stars.

teach.heading: Does the order matter?
bullets: Count the stars in a line.
Now count them in a circle.
teach.note: Rearrange the same 5 objects. Ask: is it still 5? Children need to learn that arrangement does not change the number.

practice: Count 4 blocks together while the teacher moves them.
Show me 3 fingers. Now 5 fingers.
How many eyes do you have? How many hands?
independent: Find 5 small things at home (spoons, pens, toys) and count them aloud.
Count how many cushions or chairs are in the room.
Draw 4 circles on paper and count them.
exit: Hold up 4 fingers. How many am I holding?
Count these 5 stars aloud with me.
lessons.homework: Count the shoes by your front door and tell a grown-up how many there are.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use real objects, point and count slowly, and repeat number names in the home language too. Stretch: count 6 to 10 objects.

lessons.title: Recognising the numerals 1 to 5
objectives: Recognise the numerals 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5
Match a numeral to a quantity

keywords.def: the symbol we write for a number, like 3
put together two things that go together

starter: Bismillah. Count the 4 apples on the screen.

teach.heading: Numbers have shapes
bullets: This is the numeral 1: one straight line.
This is the numeral 2: it has a curve and a flat bottom.
teach.note: Model each numeral with a large drawing. Children trace in the air with a finger, then on the table. Say the number name as you trace.

teach.heading: 3, 4 and 5
bullets: 5 has a hat and a belly.
teach.note: Use simple memory hooks. Accept any helpful hook the children invent. Watch for reversals of 3, 5 and 2 which are very common at this age.

teach.heading: Match number to amount
bullets: Does it match? Count to check.
teach.note: Show a numeral card and ask children to hold up that many fingers. Check by counting aloud together.

teach.heading: Which numeral is it?
teach.note: Show groups of 1 to 5 stars and three numeral cards. Children choose. Ask why they chose it.

practice: Point to the numeral 2 on the number line.
I will show you a numeral. Hold up that many fingers: 3, then 5, then 1.
Count the dots on the card and say the numeral.
independent: Trace the numerals 1 to 5 with a finger on a tray of flour or on the table.
Write the numeral 3 in the air, on your hand and on paper.
Match 5 number cards to groups of toys.
exit: Hold up the number of fingers that this numeral shows. (show 2)
lessons.homework: Look for numerals around the house (clock, remote, door numbers) and tell us one you found.
lessons.send: SEND: use large tactile numerals (sand, textured paper). EAL: pair numerals with pictures. Stretch: write numerals 6 to 10.

lessons.title: Seeing 1, 2 and 3 without counting
objectives: Recognise small quantities up to 3 at a glance
Say how many without counting one by one

keywords.def: knowing how many in a group straight away

starter: Show me the numeral 4 in the air.

teach.heading: Quick look!
bullets: I will show you dots for a moment.
Tell me how many without counting.
teach.note: Flash a dot card of 2 for about 2 seconds, then hide it. Ask how many they saw and how they know. This is subitising.

teach.heading: One, two, three dots
teach.note: Show the standard dice-like patterns. Name the pattern. Children say the number straight away.

teach.heading: Show me with fingers
bullets: Show me the same number on your fingers.
teach.note: Children copy the number of dots using fingers. Praise quick, correct answers and encourage honest checking.

teach.heading: Different patterns, same number
teach.note: Show two arrangements of 3. Ask which is easier to see quickly. Discuss that the number stays the same.

practice: Quick look: 2 dots. How many?
Quick look: 3 dots in a line. How many?
Quick look: 1 dot. How many?
independent: Roll a dice that only goes to 3 (or use paper cards) and say the number without counting.
Make 2 with your fingers, then 3, then 1.
Draw 3 dots in two different ways.
lessons.homework: Play 'quick look' with a grown-up: they show 1, 2 or 3 fingers fast, and you say how many.
lessons.send: SEND: allow longer viewing time. EAL: use gestures with number words. Stretch: quick look at 4 dots in a square.

lessons.title: Seeing 4 and 5, and counting out
objectives: Recognise 4 and 5 in familiar patterns
Count out a requested number of objects up to 5

keywords.def: take exactly the number of things that you are asked for

starter: Bismillah. Quick look: how many dots? (2, then 3)

teach.heading: Four dots
bullets: Quick look and say how many.
teach.note: Show 4 dots in a square, flash briefly. Ask children to describe what they saw (2 and 2).

teach.heading: Five dots
bullets: 5 dots can look like a dice face.
teach.note: Link 5 to the fingers on one hand. This supports later number bonds. Show the dice pattern with a dot in the middle.

teach.heading: Give me 4
bullets: Take them one at a time and count.
teach.note: Model counting out aloud. Emphasise stopping at the number asked for. Common error: continuing to take more.

teach.heading: Give me 5
teach.note: Children use real objects at home: raisins, buttons, paper circles. Ask the child to explain how they know it is 5.

practice: Count out 4 blocks.
Count out 2 and then 5 counters.
Quick look at 5 dots: how many?
independent: Take 5 toys to your camera and count them.
Ask a grown-up for a number from 1 to 5 and count out that many objects.
Draw 4 flowers and 5 stars.
lessons.homework: Set the table pretend-style: put out 4 spoons and 4 plates and count them.
lessons.send: SEND: use a counting tray with spaces for each object. Stretch: count out 6, 7 or 8 objects.

lessons.title: Counting to 10
objectives: Count to 10 in order
Count 6 to 10 objects accurately

keywords.def: the number after nine; all of our fingers

teach.heading: Two hands make ten
teach.note: Show both hands. Count fingers slowly, then quicker. Ask what comes after 5 and after 9.

teach.heading: Counting 6 to 10
bullets: Say it in a loud voice, then a whisper.
teach.note: Use a number rhyme or chant. Many children jump from 7 to 9 so go slowly. Use a number track on screen.

teach.heading: Count 8 things
teach.note: Remind children of one touch for one thing. Ask them to say how many there are altogether.

teach.heading: Counting backwards from 5
teach.note: Fold fingers down as you count back. Keep it playful. Do not expect full fluency yet.

practice: Count to 10 together slowly.
Count 6 blocks, then 9 blocks.
What number comes after 7? After 9?
independent: Count to 10 on your fingers three times.
Find 10 objects and put them in two rows of 5.
Count backwards from 5 to 1.
exit: How many fingers on two hands?
lessons.homework: Count the stairs, steps or tiles in your home up to 10 and tell us what you counted.
lessons.send: SEND: use a number track with big steps. EAL: chant the numbers in English and the home language. Stretch: count to 20.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Comparing and one more, one less
lessons.title: More, fewer and the same
objectives: Compare two groups using more, fewer and the same
Match one-to-one to compare

keywords.def: a bigger number of things
a smaller number of things
equal in number

teach.heading: Which group has more?
teach.note: Show two groups on the screen. Count each. Ask which number is bigger. Introduce the words 'more' and 'fewer' together.

teach.heading: Match them up
bullets: Pair one red car with one blue car.
The one with left over has more.
teach.note: Draw lines or use animation to pair items. Left-over items show which group has more without counting.

teach.heading: Fewer
teach.note: Use 'fewer' for things we can count. Mention children might say 'less' - that is fine in Reception but model 'fewer'.

teach.heading: The same
bullets: Pair them up. None left over.
teach.note: Show equal groups, then ask what we could do to make unequal groups equal.

practice: Group A has 2 stars and group B has 4 stars. Which has more?
Group A has 5 dots and group B has 3 dots. Which has fewer?
Show two groups of 3. Are they the same?
independent: Put 3 spoons in one pile and 5 in another. Which has more?
Make two groups that are the same number.
Draw one group of 2 and one of 4. Say which has fewer.
exit: 4 stars and 2 stars: which group has more?
lessons.homework: Compare the number of books and the number of toys on a shelf: which group has more?
lessons.send: SEND: keep groups small and use physical matching. Stretch: compare groups up to 10 and say how many more.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Comparing and one more, one less
lessons.title: One more
objectives: Find one more than a number up to 5
Say the number that comes next

keywords.def: add one to a group; the next number

teach.heading: Add one
teach.note: Use moving counters on screen. Say the full sentence: 2 and one more is 3.

teach.heading: The next number
bullets: One more is the next number.
teach.note: Use a number track. Point to the number and then to the next. Link one more to counting forward by one.

teach.heading: One more than 4
teach.note: Children may recount from 1 every time. Encourage counting on from 4 once they are ready.

teach.heading: Story: more dates
bullets: His mum gives him one more.
teach.note: Use a simple sharing context. Ask what we can say about Ali's dates now.

practice: What is one more than 1?
I have 3 blocks. I add one more. How many now?
What is one more than 4?
independent: Put 2 objects down. Add one more. How many now?
Do the same starting with 3, then 4.
Draw 3 circles and then one more circle.
lessons.homework: Build a tower of 2 blocks. Add one more. Tell a grown-up how many blocks you have now.
lessons.send: SEND: use a physical number track. Stretch: one more than numbers to 10.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Comparing and one more, one less
lessons.title: One less
objectives: Find one less than a number up to 5
Count backwards by one

keywords.def: take one away; the number before

starter: Bismillah. What is one more than 3?

teach.heading: Take one away
teach.note: Move one counter off the screen. Say: 4, and one less is 3. Count what is left.

teach.heading: The number before
bullets: One less is the number before.
teach.note: Use a number track and move backwards one step. Contrast with the previous lesson.

teach.heading: One more or one less?
teach.note: Ask children to show both with fingers. Mix the questions to check they listen for more or less.

teach.heading: Story: eating a date
teach.note: Use a story. Remind about saying Bismillah before eating and Alhamdulillah after - a natural link for adab.

practice: What is one less than 3?
I have 5 stars. I take one away. How many now?
What is one less than 2?
independent: Put 4 objects down, take one away, count what is left.
Do the same with 5, then 3.
Draw 5 stars and cross out one.
exit: What is one more than 2 and one less than 2?
lessons.homework: Count your toys in a row. Take one away and say how many are left.
lessons.send: SEND: use fewer objects and a single clear action. Stretch: one less and one more for numbers to 10.

lessons.title: Naming 2D shapes
objectives: Name a circle, triangle, square and rectangle
Say how many sides some shapes have

keywords.def: a round shape with no corners
a shape with 3 straight sides
a shape with 4 equal sides
a shape with 4 sides and 4 corners

starter: Bismillah. What is one more than 2?

teach.heading: Circle
teach.note: Show real objects: a plate, a coin, a clock. Children trace a circle in the air.

teach.heading: Triangle
teach.note: Count the sides by tracing. Show triangles in different orientations and sizes to avoid the idea that a triangle must point upwards.

teach.heading: Square and rectangle
bullets: A rectangle has 4 sides: 2 long, 2 short.
teach.note: Compare a window or book with a tile or square cracker. Do not expect every child to separate them yet; say that a square is a special rectangle later on.

teach.heading: Shape hunt
bullets: Find a circle, a triangle, a rectangle.
teach.note: Children search nearby and bring or point to a shape. Praise accurate naming.

practice: Which shape is round with no corners?
How many sides does a triangle have?
Is a door a circle or a rectangle?
independent: Find 3 circles at home and say what they are.
Draw a triangle, a square and a rectangle.
Make a triangle with 3 straws, sticks or pencils.
exit: What is this shape called? (show triangle)
How many corners does a square have?
lessons.homework: Go on a shape hunt at home. Find one circle, one rectangle and one square.
lessons.send: SEND: use real objects and touch the edges. EAL: pair each shape name with a picture. Stretch: name a hexagon and a pentagon.

lessons.title: Sorting and building with shapes
objectives: Sort shapes by one feature
Make a picture using 2D shapes

keywords.def: put things into groups that are the same in some way
a straight edge of a shape

starter: How many sides does a triangle have?

teach.heading: Sorting shapes
bullets: Put the shapes with corners together.
teach.note: Use cut-out shapes on screen. Ask why each shape goes where it goes. Accept any sensible sorting rule.

teach.heading: Sort by size or colour
bullets: Sort big shapes and small shapes.
teach.note: Show that the same shapes can be sorted in different ways. Keep to one rule per sort to avoid confusion.

teach.heading: Build a house
teach.note: Model building a picture from shapes. Name each shape as you place it and count how many shapes you used.

teach.heading: Tell us about your picture
teach.note: Children share their pictures. Ask them to name and count one type of shape.

practice: Sort these shapes into circles and not circles.
I need a shape for a wheel. Which shape?
Which two shapes make a rocket?
independent: Build a house or a boat from paper shapes.
Sort your shapes into two groups and explain your rule.
Count how many triangles you used.
exit: Name two shapes you used in your picture.
lessons.homework: Make a picture from at least three different shapes (cut paper or draw) and bring it to show us.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-cut large shapes or use a magnetic shape set. Stretch: describe each shape using the words side and corner.

lessons.title: Making and continuing patterns
objectives: Spot a repeating pattern
Copy, continue and make an ABAB pattern

keywords.def: something that repeats in the same order
do the same thing again

starter: Bismillah. Name these shapes: circle, square, triangle.

teach.heading: What is a pattern?
teach.note: Show a red-blue-red-blue line of beads. Pause before the last item and ask the children to predict.

teach.heading: Clap a pattern
teach.note: Use sound patterns as well as visual ones. Children copy with claps and taps. Patterns are everywhere: tiles, carpets, prayer mats.

teach.heading: Continue the pattern
teach.note: Show a line with a gap or an unfinished end. Ask children to say what comes next and why.

teach.heading: Make your own
bullets: Put them in a repeating line.
teach.note: Use objects at home: a spoon and a fork, a pen and a rubber. Mention the beautiful repeating patterns in Islamic art as an example of pattern, without further claims.

practice: Red, yellow, red, yellow, ... what comes next?
Square, triangle, square, ... what comes next?
Clap, clap, tap, clap, clap, ... what comes next?
independent: Make an ABAB pattern with two kinds of toys.
Draw a pattern using two colours.
Make a pattern of claps and taps for a grown-up to copy.
exit: Blue, green, blue, green, ... what comes next?
Can you make a pattern with your fingers?
lessons.homework: Find a pattern at home (on a carpet, a plate, clothes) and tell us about it.
lessons.send: SEND: start with a physical line of two objects. Stretch: make an AAB or ABC pattern.

lessons.title: Numbers to 10 review and games
objectives: Show what we know about counting, comparing and shapes
Play number games with confidence

keywords.def: how many there are altogether

starter: What is one more than 4? One less than 3?
Name a circle, a triangle and a rectangle.

teach.heading: Counting game
teach.note: Show cards from 1 to 8. Children count out objects and check each other. Celebrate effort and honesty.

teach.heading: Which is more?
teach.note: Use pairs like 3 and 5, 4 and 2, 7 and 6. Ask how they know.

teach.heading: Shape and pattern quiz
teach.note: Quick-fire. Use visual cards on the screen. Make it feel like a game, not a test.

teach.heading: Thank Allah for what we learnt
bullets: We can compare and make patterns.
teach.note: Brief reflection. Invite children to share one thing they enjoyed learning about numbers.

practice: Count out 7 counters.
Which is one more than 6?
Which shape has 3 sides?
independent: Play a number hunt: find 1 of something, 2 of something, up to 5 of something.
Draw your favourite pattern.
Count your fingers and toes.
lessons.homework: Teach a grown-up or sibling one thing you learnt in maths this month.
lessons.send: SEND: choose the games that match each child's current stage; use praise for effort. Stretch: counting on from a number other than one.
